pos: n. pl. (those who humbly entreat; worshippers who make supplication)
etymology: From French suppliant, from Latin supplicare, to kneel down, to entreat humbly, from sub, under, and plicare, to fold or bend. The Hebrew athar means worshippers or those who pray.
biblical_def: Zephaniah's prophecy of judgment ends with a burst of promise. God will turn to the peoples a pure language, “that they may all call upon the name of the LORD, to serve him with one consent” (Zephaniah 3:9). Then: “From beyond the rivers of Ethiopia my suppliants, even the daughter of my dispersed, shall bring mine offering.” From the farthest edge of the known world, beyond the rivers of Cush, worshippers will come to the LORD with offerings. They are called His suppliants, those who pray to Him, and the daughter of His dispersed, His scattered people gathered home. The prophecy began to be fulfilled when the Ethiopian eunuch, returning from worship at Jerusalem, believed the gospel and was baptized (Acts 8:27-39), and it continues wherever the nations call upon the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. The gospel creates a people from every nation who come not with the pride of the builders of Babel but as humble suppliants, bowing before the one true God. The reversal of Babel's confusion begins at Pentecost and will be complete when every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord.

pos: n. pl. (forefathers; ancestors in the direct line)
etymology: From Latin progenitor, an ancestor, from progignere, to beget, from pro, forth, and gignere, to beget. The Hebrew horay means those who conceived me, my parents.
biblical_def: As Jacob lay dying in Egypt, he blessed each of his sons. To Joseph, the son who had been sold, imprisoned and exalted, he gave a blessing overflowing with abundance, ending: “The blessings of thy father have prevailed above the blessings of my progenitors unto the utmost bound of the everlasting hills: they shall be on the head of Joseph, and on the crown of the head of him that was separate from his brethren.” Jacob had received the blessing of Isaac, who had received the blessing of Abraham. Now Jacob declares that the blessings he passes on exceed even those of his fathers, reaching to the utmost bound of the everlasting hills. The covenant promise grew as it passed down the generations. Joseph, separated from his brethren by their envy, received the crown of blessing, a type of Christ, who was rejected by His brethren and exalted to the right hand of God. The verse also teaches that faith is passed from fathers to sons, and that each generation stands upon the blessings of its progenitors while looking forward to the greater blessing God has promised.

etymology: From woman, Old English wifman, and kind, Old English cynd, nature or race. The Hebrew phrase is literally the lyings of a woman.
biblical_def: Leviticus 18 lists the sexual relations forbidden to Israel, practices for which the Canaanites were being driven out of the land. Among them stands this command: “Thou shalt not lie with mankind, as with womankind: it is abomination.” The verse assumes the creational order of Genesis 1:27, “male and female created he them,” and Genesis 2:24, where a man cleaves to his wife and they become one flesh. Sexual union is designed for a man and a woman within marriage; to lie with a man as with a woman is to violate that design, and God calls it abomination. The New Testament confirms the prohibition: Paul names it among the sins of those who exchanged the truth of God for a lie (Romans 1:26-27) and among the sins that exclude from the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:9-10). Yet the same passage proclaims hope: “And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11). The word womankind thus stands within God's good order for the sexes, which His law protects and His gospel restores.

corruption_paragraphs: Revisionist interpreters argue that the Levitical prohibition addresses only temple prostitution, pederasty or abusive relationships, and that the ceremonial law no longer binds Christians. But the text forbids the act itself, without qualification, and the New Testament repeats the prohibition in moral, not ceremonial, contexts (Romans 1; 1 Corinthians 6; 1 Timothy 1:10).

The dictionary holds the biblical sexual ethic: marriage between one man and one woman is the only legitimate setting for sexual union, grounded in creation. The church calls all sinners, of every kind, to repentance and offers them full cleansing in Christ, distinguishing pastoral care for the person from approval of the sin.

etymology: From Old French galant, present participle of galer, to make merry or show off. The Hebrew addir means majestic or mighty.
biblical_def: Isaiah 33 describes the security of Zion under the reign of the LORD. Jerusalem had no great river like the Nile or the Euphrates to defend it, but the LORD Himself would be its defence: “But there the glorious LORD will be unto us a place of broad rivers and streams; wherein shall go no galley with oars, neither shall gallant ship pass thereby.” Broad rivers protected a city, but they also carried enemy warships. The rivers of God's presence protect without that danger, for no galley with oars and no gallant warship can sail on them to attack. The next verse gives the reason: “For the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us” (Isaiah 33:22). The glory of the LORD is the defence of His people. The gallant ships of empire, stately and powerful, cannot touch the city where He reigns. The New Testament fulfilment is the heavenly Jerusalem, through which flows “a pure river of water of life” (Revelation 22:1), and where the redeemed dwell secure forever.

biblical_def: When Abraham's servant had found Rebekah and she had consented to go with him to be Isaac's wife, her family sent her away with a blessing: “And they blessed Rebekah, and said unto her, Thou art our sister, be thou the mother of thousands of millions, and let thy seed possess the gate of those which hate them.” Without knowing it, they echoed the oath God had sworn to Abraham after the offering of Isaac: “thy seed shall possess the gate of his enemies” (Genesis 22:17). Rebekah would become the mother of Jacob, and through him of Israel, a nation as the stars of heaven. But the deeper fulfilment is in the one Seed, Christ (Galatians 3:16), whose people are “a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Revelation 7:9). The gate of the enemy is possessed when Christ triumphs over sin, death and Satan, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against His church (Matthew 16:18). Rebekah's blessing reached far beyond what her brothers understood.

pos: v.t. (to call back to mind; to remember)
etymology: From re-, back, and call, from Old Norse kalla. The Hebrew phrase is literally I cause to return to my heart.
biblical_def: Lamentations 3 is the lament of a man who has seen affliction by the rod of God's wrath. He has been walled in, his prayers shut out, his teeth broken with gravel stones; he says, “My strength and my hope is perished from the LORD” (3:18). Then the turning point: “This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope.” What he calls to mind follows at once: “It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness” (3:22-23). Nothing in his circumstances had changed; Jerusalem still lay in ruins. What changed was what he deliberately brought back to his heart. Hope did not come from feelings but from remembering the character of God. This is the discipline of faith in suffering: to preach to oneself the truth of God's steadfast love when everything visible contradicts it. The psalmist does the same: “Why art thou cast down, O my soul? ... hope thou in God” (Psalm 42:5). Believers recall God's mercies supremely at the cross, where His compassion and faithfulness are displayed beyond all doubt.

pos: adj. (dark and threatening, as a stormy sky)
etymology: From Middle English louren, to frown or scowl, related to Middle Dutch loeren, to lurk. Not related to lower, to let down. Christ's Greek stugnazo means to be gloomy or overcast.
biblical_def: The Pharisees and Sadducees came to Jesus demanding a sign from heaven. He answered, “When it is evening, ye say, It will be fair weather: for the sky is red” (Matthew 16:2), and then: “And in the morning, It will be foul weather to day: for the sky is red and lowring. O ye hypocrites, ye can discern the face of the sky; but can ye not discern the signs of the times?” They were skilled weather-watchers, reading a red evening sky as fair and a red, lowring morning sky as storm. Yet the greatest sign in history stood before them, the Messiah doing the works foretold by the prophets, and they could not see it. Their problem was not lack of evidence but lack of willingness; they asked for a sign while rejecting the signs already given. Christ refused them any sign but that of the prophet Jonas (Matthew 16:4), His own death and resurrection. The lowring sky also warned of judgment. Within a generation the storm broke upon Jerusalem. The lesson stands: men who can forecast tomorrow's weather often cannot discern the most urgent spiritual realities.

pos: n. (the hinder part of a ship)
etymology: From Middle English sterne, probably from Old Norse stjorn, steering, the place where the ship was steered. Luke's Greek prumna means the stern or hinder part.
biblical_def: Paul's voyage to Rome ran into the great tempest Euroclydon. For fourteen days the ship was driven, and on the fourteenth night the sailors sensed land near. Sounding, they found the water growing shallower: “Then fearing lest we should have fallen upon rocks, they cast four anchors out of the stern, and wished for the day.” Anchoring from the stern held the ship pointed toward the shore, ready to run aground at daybreak. The sailors then tried to flee in the boat under pretence of casting anchors out of the foreship, but Paul warned the centurion, “Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved” (Acts 27:31). God had already promised Paul that there would be no loss of any man's life (27:22), yet the means mattered; the sailors had to remain. This is a striking picture of God's sovereignty and human responsibility working together. The promise was certain, and the anchors, the sailors and the daylight were the means God used to fulfil it. In the end, “so it came to pass, that they escaped all safe to land” (27:44). Hebrews calls the believer's hope “an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast” (Hebrews 6:19).

etymology: From Old English weod, a herb or grass, later any unwanted plant. In Jonah the Hebrew suph means reeds or seaweed, the same word in the name of the Red Sea, Yam Suph.
biblical_def: From the belly of the great fish, Jonah prayed, recalling how close he had come to death in the depths: “The waters compassed me about, even to the soul: the depth closed me round about, the weeds were wrapped about my head.” He had sunk to the bottoms of the mountains, the seaweed tangling his head like a burial shroud. “The earth with her bars was about me for ever: yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption, O LORD my God” (Jonah 2:6). Jonah's prayer is full of the language of the Psalms, and it ends with the confession that is the heart of the book: “Salvation is of the LORD” (2:9). The Lord Jesus took Jonah's descent and deliverance as the sign of His own death and resurrection: “For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40). Christ went down into the true depths of death and the grave, not for His own disobedience as Jonah had, but for the sins of His people, and God brought up His life from corruption.

The dictionary affirms the historicity of Jonah as Christ did. The weeds wrapped about the prophet's head are the real terror of a real man in the depths, and his deliverance is a true sign of the greater deliverance of Christ from the grave.

etymology: From un-, not, and shod, past participle of shoe, Old English scoh. The Hebrew means bare or barefoot.
biblical_def: Jeremiah 2 is God's lawsuit against Judah for forsaking Him to run after idols. Like a wild ass in heat that cannot be restrained, Judah chased her lovers. The LORD warns her: “Withhold thy foot from being unshod, and thy throat from thirst: but thou saidst, There is no hope: no; for I have loved strangers, and after them will I go.” The picture is of a woman running so recklessly after her lovers that she wears out her shoes and parches her throat. God pleads with her to stop before she is ruined. But Judah answers with the despairing defiance of the addicted heart: “There is no hope: no.” She does not mean that God offers no hope; she means that she will not give up her idols. It is the voice of every sinner who loves his sin too much to leave it. Yet God's plea in the same chapter is full of grief: “my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters” (Jeremiah 2:13). The fountain stands open. The sinner's cry “There is no hope” is answered by the gospel: the God he has forsaken still calls him to return.

corruption_summary: Bondage to sin is redefined as identity or incurable compulsion, echoing Judah's cry, There is no hope, instead of hearing God's call to forsake idols and return.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern culture often treats besetting sins as fixed identities or as compulsions beyond the reach of moral responsibility. The sinner is told that he is simply wired this way, and the call to repentance is heard as cruelty. Judah's answer, There is no hope: no, for I have loved strangers, is the ancient form of the same surrender.

Scripture names the bondage honestly and names the remedy just as plainly. The heart that loves its idols is truly enslaved, yet God calls it to return to the fountain of living waters. In Christ there is power to break the dominion of sin (Romans 6:14).
